title: Recovering data layout from address arithmetic
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read an element size, a field offset and a field width out of a single instruction, and reconstruct a structure definition from a binary that carries no type information.

blocks.text: A compiled binary contains no types. What it contains is address arithmetic, and address arithmetic is a faithful record of the layout the types described. Reading it backwards is one of the most useful skills in this course.

blocks.caption: One instruction, three facts
lines: struct Point { int x, y; };
int pt_y(struct Point *p, long i) { return p[i].y; }
mov eax, dword ptr [rdi + 8*rsi + 4]
|        offset of the field: 4
size of one element: 8
One instruction states the entire layout: elements are 8 bytes apart, the
field being read is 4 bytes in, and it is 4 bytes wide (dword ptr).
That is sizeof(struct Point) == 8 and offsetof(y) == 4, recovered from
a binary with no source and no debug information.

blocks.title: The three pieces and what each tells you
blocks.text: The scale is the size of one array element. The displacement is the offset of the field within the element. The size annotation — byte, word, dword, qword — is the width of the field itself. Read those three from any array access and you have a row of the structure definition. Do it for every field the program touches and you have most of the structure.

blocks.caption: A structure that is bigger than its contents
lines: struct Big { long a; int b; char c; };     /* 8 + 4 + 1 = 13 bytes of data */
long big_a(struct Big *b, long i) { return b[i].a; }
shl rsi, 4                             ; i * 16
mov rax, qword ptr [rdi + rsi]         ; field a at offset 0
char big_c(struct Big *b, long i) { return b[i].c; }
shl   rsi, 4                           ; i * 16
movsx eax, byte ptr [rdi + rsi + 12]   ; field c at offset 12
Confirmed by running the program: sizeof(Big) = 16, offsetof(c) = 12.
/* The struct holds 13 bytes of data and occupies 16. Three bytes of tail
padding keep the 8-byte field aligned in the next element. And note the
shl instead of a scale: the addressing mode allows only 1, 2, 4 and 8,
so any element size outside that set needs a separate multiply or shift.
Seeing shl rsi, 4 followed by [base + rsi] means elements of 16 bytes. */

blocks.text: The C course explained alignment as a rule about where fields may sit. Here it is as a consequence you can measure: a structure declaring thirteen bytes of fields occupies sixteen, and the binary states both numbers plainly. If you reconstruct a structure and your calculated size does not match the stride the code uses, padding is the first thing to suspect and reordering the fields is the usual explanation.
When the element size is not 1, 2, 4 or 8

rows: The scale in the addressing mode; no extra instruction
shl to multiply, then a plain base+index
lea combinations, or imul for awkward sizes

blocks.text: Each row leaves a distinct fingerprint. A shl by 4 before an array access means sixteen-byte elements. An imul by 24 means a structure of three eight-byte fields. An imul by a register means the stride is a variable, which usually means a manually indexed two-dimensional array or a runtime-sized element.

blocks.caption: A fixed row length against a runtime one
lines: int m2d(int (*m)[16], long i, long j) { return m[i][j]; }
shl rsi, 6                            ; i * 64 -- 16 ints per row
add rsi, rdi
mov eax, dword ptr [rsi + 4*rdx]      ; + j * 4
int m2d_var(int *m, long cols, long i, long j) { return m[i*cols + j]; }
imul rsi, rdx                         ; a REAL multiply
lea  rax, [rdi + 4*rsi]
mov  eax, dword ptr [rax + 4*rcx]
/* Same access, two costs. When the row length is part of the type the
compiler knows it at compile time and uses a shift; when it is a runtime
value it must multiply. That is one reason a fixed-size 2D array can be
faster than a pointer-plus-stride one, and it is visible in the binary. */

blocks.title: The row length is the thing to find first
blocks.text: When reading unfamiliar code that walks a two-dimensional structure, identify the row stride before anything else. It tells you the width of the data, which usually tells you what the data is. A stride of 64 bytes with 4-byte elements is a 16-wide array; a stride of 3 bytes is very likely an image in 24-bit colour; a stride matching a page size suggests something aligned deliberately.

blocks.caption: Two source forms that often compile to the same thing
lines: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) s += a[i];      /* indexing */
while (p < end)         s += *p++;      /* pointer walking */
Both typically become:
add  eax, dword ptr [rdi + 4*rcx]
inc  rcx
cmp  rsi, rcx
jne  .Lbody
/* The compiler chooses whichever induction variable produces better code
and freely converts between the two forms. Writing pointer arithmetic
by hand for speed was worthwhile decades ago; today it mostly costs
readability and changes nothing in the output. Check before believing
otherwise -- the disassembly settles it in seconds. */

items: Find every access whose base is the same pointer
Record each one's scale, displacement and size annotation
The largest scale, or the shl/imul preceding the accesses, is the element size
Sort the displacements: those are the field offsets
The size annotation at each offset is that field's width
Check for gaps — a gap is padding, and it constrains the alignment of the next field
Check whether a field is read with movsx or movzx: signed or unsigned

blocks.text: That procedure produces a structure definition accurate enough to write in C and use, without ever seeing the original header. It is the everyday work of reverse engineering, and the only part that requires judgement is naming the fields — which the binary cannot tell you and which is why symbol names, when a binary still carries them, are so valuable.

blocks.title: Reconstruct a structure you did not define
steps: Define a structure with fields of mixed sizes and write four accessor functions
Compile at -O1 and record the scale, displacement and size for each accessor
From those numbers alone, write down what you think the structure is
Compare with your definition, including the padding
Add a printf of sizeof and offsetof to confirm the sizes you inferred
Reorder the fields to remove padding and recompile; watch the scale change
Write both an indexed and a pointer-walking loop and compare the assembly
Write a 2D access with a fixed row length and a runtime one, and find the shl and the imul
blocks.expected: A reconstructed definition that matches, a stride that shrinks when you reorder the fields, and identical assembly from the two loop forms. The reorder step is worth doing twice: it is the same field-ordering advice the C course gave for saving memory, and here you can watch it change the generated code.

cheatsheet: A memory operand states three facts: element size (scale), field offset (displacement), field width (size annotation)
mov eax, dword ptr [rdi + 8*rsi + 4] means 8-byte elements, field at offset 4, 4 bytes wide
Scale supports only 1, 2, 4 and 8; other element sizes need shl or imul first
shl by 4 before an access means 16-byte elements
imul by a register means the stride is a runtime value
A struct declaring 13 bytes can occupy 16; the padding is visible as the stride
Fixed-length rows compile to a shift; runtime row lengths compile to a multiply
Find the row stride first when reading unfamiliar two-dimensional code
Indexed loops and pointer-walking loops usually compile to the same instructions
movsx versus movzx at a field tells you whether it is signed

checkpoint.prompt: You see mov eax, dword ptr [rdi + 8*rsi + 4]. What does it tell you about the data?

choices.A: Only that it is an array — nothing about the fields
choices.D: 8-byte stride; field 4 bytes into each element

checkpoint.explanation: Scale, displacement and size annotation give element size, field offset and field width — one row of the structure definition, from one instruction.

checkpoint.prompt: An access is preceded by shl rsi, 4 and then uses [rdi + rsi + 12]. What are the element size and field offset?
checkpoint.explanation: The addressing mode allows scales of 1, 2, 4 and 8 only. Any other element size appears as a separate shift or multiply, which is itself the clue.

checkpoint.prompt: A struct declares long a; int b; char c; — thirteen bytes of fields — but the stride is 16. Why?

choices.A: The compiler reserved space for future fields it might add
choices.B: Sixteen is the minimum struct size
choices.C: Padding — to align the next element's 8-byte field
choices.D: The char is stored as an int

checkpoint.explanation: Confirmed by running the program: sizeof is 16 and offsetof(c) is 12. If a reconstructed size does not match the stride, padding is the first suspect.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does m[i][j] with a fixed row length compile to shl while m[i*cols + j] compiles to imul?

choices.D: A fixed row length is known at compile time so the multiply becomes a shift

checkpoint.explanation: A runtime row length must actually be multiplied. Same access, two costs, and the difference is visible in the binary. It is one reason a fixed-size two-dimensional array can outperform a pointer-plus-stride one.
